That requires the expected absolute value to be finite.

Let Y be another discrete random variable with finite expectation.
Then the absolute value of X is integrable.
Then the absolute value of Y is integrable.
The triangle inequality gives a bound for the absolute value of X plus Y.
Specifically, the absolute value of X plus Y is at most the sum of the absolute values.
The sum of two integrable random variables is integrable.
Therefore X plus Y has finite expected absolute value.
Therefore the expectation of X plus Y exists as a finite number.
In that setting, the expectation of X plus Y equals the sum of the expectations.
So no example exists under the usual definition.
A common source of confusion is the extended expectation convention.
There, one may assign plus infinity or minus infinity to some variables.
But a finite expected value still rules out both positive and negative infinity parts.
If either variable had an undefined expectation, the question would change.
If either variable had an infinite expected value, the question would change.
The stated condition requires both expectations to be finite.
Under that condition, the sum expectation cannot be undefined or infinite.
